title: 1.1 What is GIS?
text:
The concept of ‘space’ is part of much research in the humanities and in linguistics. Archaeological finds, historical events and linguistic phenomena, among others, are partly defined by their location and distribution. Because of this, these disciplines often need to structure, analyse and visualise information spatially. This can be done in different ways: analogue or digital, with general tools or with specialised tools.
Geographic information systems (GIS) belong to this last category. These (digital) systems were developed specifically to process geo-information, that is, information with a spatial dimension.
Geographic information systems offer their users a wide range of tools and functions that can relate to every step of the data processing workflow:







1.
Creating digital geodata (manually or automatically)


2.
Structuring, modelling, storing and managing spatial information


3.
Editing both the spatial and the non-spatial information


4.
Querying geographic data


5.
Visualising and exporting maps



Not every GIS application covers all of the aspects above. There is a great variety of GIS software: some packages specialise in specific aspects (for example storing geodata or creating maps), others take a more integrated approach.
There are also large differences in user interaction: some applications have an advanced graphical user interface, others have none at all.
Finally, there are applications meant for local use (desktop software) as well as server-based systems. The latter offer extra possibilities (for example for collaboration), but they also require a lot of system administration work. For this reason, they are usually out of reach for individual researchers.

title: 1.1 What is GIS?
text:
Desktop GIS
In this very diverse GIS landscape, ArcGIS and QGIS are among the most widely used software packages. Both offer a wide range of functions in an integrated, user-friendly graphical interface. Both can also easily be installed as a standalone application on the end user’s computer. Because they are fairly easy to learn, easy to install and offer many possibilities, these packages have helped to make GIS popular in the humanities and in linguistics.
The basic principles of ArcGIS and QGIS are the same:

The map canvas of these GIS applications can be seen as a coordinate system.
On this coordinate system, (spatial) information can be positioned based on an x value and a y value (in a geographic coordinate system, these are the longitude and the latitude, expressed in degrees; see the chapter on coordinate systems). So the data we mainly work with in a GIS environment are data that contain coordinates. If they do not, a GIS will not be able to position the data (correctly) in space. By default, the axes and the coordinate grid itself are not visible in the map canvas of these geographic information systems. However, they are still present in the background.
Non-spatial information can be linked to spatial information.
For example, you can have a data object that represents a point with the coordinates 3.723° east longitude and 51.045° north latitude (spatial information). About this point you can say that it is the Book Tower (name), that it was built in the period 1936–1942 (period) and that it is owned by Ghent University (owner). Name, construction period and owner are of course non-spatial data. Both the spatial and the non-spatial dimensions of a dataset can be queried and edited in these geographic information systems.
In these GIS environments, data are ideally stored in (one or more) thematic information layers.
Examples of such layers are roads (and waterways), buildings, boundaries, contour lines… In a GIS environment, different information layers can easily be combined, compared and processed.

Besides these general principles, ArcGIS and QGIS also have more similarities than differences in their user interface and functions. If you know one of these systems well, you will quickly learn the other one, and the other way round. Still, there are of course some (small and larger) differences in use, performance and possibilities. Neither package is better than the other in every respect: both have advantages and disadvantages.
ArcGIS (its current desktop application is called ArcGIS Pro) is a commercial product of the company Esri. To be able to use it, you therefore need to purchase a licence. QGIS, on the other hand, is open source software and completely free to use. For this reason, the practical parts of this learning path will always use QGIS.

title: 1.1 What is GIS?
text:
QGIS
To follow this learning path properly, we recommend that you install QGIS on your own computer. You can easily download it from the project website https://www.qgis.org. Choose the installer for your operating system (Windows, macOS or Linux).
The download page offers two versions: the Long Term Release (LTR), which is the most stable version, and the latest release, which has the newest functions.
GIS software evolves quickly, and new versions follow one another at a fast pace. This learning path is based on QGIS 4.x (the screenshots were made with QGIS 4.2.3). 






Changes to the functions and the interface are usually small, but even between minor versions (4.0, 4.2, …) differences occur in practice: for example, a button in a slightly different place or with a slightly different name. If your screen does not look exactly like a screenshot, look for a button or menu item with a similar name nearby.

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
When you open the software for the first time after installation, you will see the following screen:
The main window consists of several elements. Some of them are discussed in more detail later in this learning path; here we give a general overview.

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
A: Menu bar
In the menu bar, hierarchical menus give you access to a wide range of QGIS configuration options and functions: from personalising the interface to running analyses on your data.

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
B: Toolbars
The toolbars give you direct access to important and frequently used functions. Many of these are also available through the menu bar, but here they are quicker to reach and save you some mouse clicks. GIS is used for a wide variety of purposes, and not everyone needs the same tools: someone who digitises historical maps uses other functions far more often than someone who analyses statistics. That is why you can choose which toolbars are shown and where they are placed: tick the ones you want under View ▸ Toolbars, then drag them with your mouse to where you want them.
Examples of frequently used toolbars are:







Project toolbar
e.g. creating a new project and saving it


Map navigation toolbar
e.g. pan tool and zoom options


Attributes toolbar
e.g. looking up attribute information (identifying features, opening the attribute table)


Selection toolbar
e.g. selecting and deselecting features


Data source manager toolbar
e.g. adding new data to the project and creating new data layers


Digitizing toolbar
e.g. editing and adding geometries

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
C: Panels
Panels are special widgets (small windows inside the QGIS window that you can show, hide, move or dock) that let you use certain functions in your GIS environment through a visual interface. As with the toolbars, you can choose which panels are visible and where exactly they are shown: under View ▸ Panels you can switch each panel on or off. If a panel you need (for example one from the table below) is not visible on your screen, you can open it there.








C1
Browser panel
(Explorer)
The Browser panel gives you quick access to all your data sources. With this widget you can easily view and import local files on your computer as well as data on a server or in a database.


C2
Layers panel
(Table of contents)
Here you see an overview of all layers that have been imported into your GIS project. You can choose which of these layers are (in)visible in the map canvas and in which order they are shown. The Layers panel gives you access to the advanced configuration options of the different layers.


C3
Processing toolbox
In the Processing Toolbox, the available tools for analysis and data processing are grouped in thematic groups that you can expand.

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
D: Map canvas
The most eye-catching part of the interface is the map canvas. Here you can view a spatial visualisation of your geographic data (layers). The map canvas is an interactive window: as a user, you can zoom in and out, move around the map, look up information about features and select data.







NoteSee also



Zooming and panning are explained on Navigating the map canvas.

title: 1.2 QGIS interface
text:
E: Status bar
In the status bar you will find general information about your map (e.g. the coordinates your mouse is hovering over, the coordinate system used, the scale). You can also rotate your map there, so that north is no longer at the top. Finally, this bar also shows status messages about actions that are running or have finished.







NoteSee also



The status bar is explained in more detail on The status bar.

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
In GIS, you work with information that has both a spatial component (defined by coordinates) and a non-spatial component (attribute data). This information can be structured technically in different ways. The two most commonly used data models in GIS are the raster model and the vector model. They differ in how they store the spatial component and in what kind of attribute data can be linked to it. We start with the raster model.
Rasters define geographic information by means of a grid of cells (or pixels) organised in rows and columns. Below, we take a short look at some characteristics and give some examples.

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
Grid of cells
In a raster file, geographic space is divided into a matrix of cells, each covering a small part of that space. Each cell is implicitly given coordinates. The real-world size of one cell (e.g. 10 by 10 metres) is called the spatial resolution; it differs from raster file to raster file. Within one raster, however, all cells always have the same size and shape.

Data: SRTM shaded relief, USGS (public domain).
Raster files are easy to recognise: at first sight you cannot always see the individual cells, but if you zoom in far enough, the matrix of cells becomes clearly visible.

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
Numeric values
Each cell can be given one or more numeric values, which apply to the whole area covered by the cell. The unit of these values differs from raster to raster, and the options are almost unlimited. Common examples are rasters in which each cell contains the elevation or the temperature.
Although the values of raster cells are always numeric, you can also use a raster file to show textual data, by means of a code system and a legend. Take the example of the official land use map of the Flemish government. Each cell of this raster map contains a number as its value. The legend that comes with it explains that a cell with value 1 corresponds to ‘urban core buildings’, 2 to ‘other buildings’, 3 to ‘industrial and commercial infrastructure’, etc. In this way, the values in the cells are numeric, but their meaning is not.
The example below makes the logic of this system clear:








NoteSee also



How to look up the values of raster cells in QGIS is explained on Cell values: histogram and unique values.

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
Single-band and multi-band
In the example above, we looked at a simple raster file in which each pixel was given at most one numeric value. Such images are also called single-band images.
However, a raster image can also consist of several image layers (image bands). In that case, each pixel has one value per image band. All bands of one raster share exactly the same grid: the same number of rows and columns, the same cell size and the same position. You can picture them as sheets stacked on top of each other, in which every cell lies exactly above the corresponding cell in the other bands; only the values stored in the cells differ from band to band. Colour scans (e.g. a scanned historical map) and digital colour photos (e.g. aerial photos) are examples of such multi-band raster files. When an image is scanned or photographed, it is converted into a digital raster of pixels, and the scanner or camera gives each pixel a colour in the form of a numeric code. There are different ways to express colour numerically. A common one is ‘RGB’ (red - green - blue): here each pixel is given not one value but three, containing the amounts of red, green and blue that together form the colour.






A scanned map contains colours, not the values the map shows. If you scan a paper elevation map, for example, the cells of your digital raster will not contain the elevations themselves (a scanner cannot know these), but the numeric codes of the colours used on the original map.




An aerial photo (orthophoto) is a typical multi-band raster: three bands with the red, green and blue values of each cell together form the colour image. Orthophoto: Digitaal Vlaanderen, orthophoto mosaic 2025 (Ghent, Gravensteen).

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
Continuous and discrete data

Continuous data
The raster model is very suitable for representing continuous data. Continuous data are data that have no clear geographic boundaries, or only vague ones, such as air quality, temperature or elevation. If you look at the temperature map of Europe below, you will see that it contains different ‘temperature zones’. This is of course a simplification: in reality, the temperature does not jump at a sharp line from exactly 17°C in one zone to 18°C in the next. Phenomena such as temperature change gradually across space and therefore cannot be delimited precisely.
The raster model offers a good way of dealing with this difficulty. Space is systematically divided into equal parts and so simplified into a set of small, indivisible cells. This creates a predefined spatial framework in which information can be recorded. In this simplified representation of space, each cell is given a measured or estimated value that applies to the whole cell.

Mean temperature in August (1970–2000). Each cell (10 × 10 km) has one value. Data: WorldClim 2.1 (Fick & Hijmans 2017), CC BY 4.0; borders: Natural Earth.


Discrete data
Besides continuous data, rasters can also contain discrete data. These are data that can be clearly delimited, such as buildings, roads, water bodies… Think, for example, of the buildings and roads you can see on an aerial photo. In raster images, the accuracy of discrete data depends on the spatial resolution. The higher the resolution (the smaller the cells), the more detail can be shown and the more accurately boundaries can be drawn.

title: 2.1 Raster model
text:
Simple, but large files
Because the raster model is a very simple data structure, many analyses can be carried out quickly. On the other hand, the files are often large, because information has to be stored for each individual cell.

title: 2.2 Vector model
text: The second commonly used data model in GIS is the vector model. It describes geographic information as separate geometric objects (features): points, lines and areas – called polygons. The shape and position of each object are defined by coordinates: a point by one coordinate pair, a line or a polygon by the coordinates of its (corner) points – called vertices. Below, we take a short look at the main characteristics of the vector model and give some examples.

title: 2.2 Vector model
text:
Points, lines and polygons







NoteSee also



The raster model is discussed on Raster model. A comparison of both models is on Rasters vs. vectors.




Points consist of one coordinate.
Lines consist of at least two coordinates (a start point and an end point).
All points of a line, including the start and end points, are called vertices. The parts of the line between two successive vertices are called segments.
Polygons consist of a line whose start point and end point are the same.
The whole area enclosed by this line also belongs to the polygon. A polygon needs at least four coordinates (a triangle): three different points, plus the first point repeated as the end point.

title: 2.2 Vector model
text:
Very accurate
As you learned on the previous page, data in the raster model are positioned in space by means of a grid of cells. Vector objects, on the other hand, are positioned in space by means of exact coordinates. So, unlike with rasters, there is no generalisation to a grid of cells. In other words, vectors are not resolution-dependent. This also has visual consequences: no matter how far you zoom in on a vector object, the object will always be shown sharply. Technically, there is no limit to the level of detail you can work with. In practice, of course, the accuracy depends on how precisely the data were drawn.
Because vector objects have exact positions and sharp boundaries, they are very suitable for storing discrete data, but less suitable for continuous data.

title: 2.2 Vector model
text:
Attribute data
Another important difference from the raster model is that a variety of attribute data can be linked to vector objects. Besides numbers (whole or decimal), these can also be text or dates, for example. Moreover, while a raster cell in practice usually holds only one value (or a few), vector objects often have many attribute fields.
The example below shows a vector file with point objects that represent cities. Each vector object – also called a feature – contains several attribute fields: the city’s name (text), the number of inhabitants (a whole number), the area of its territory (decimal number), and the region it belongs to (text).

In QGIS and similar programs, you can consult the attribute data of a single feature directly in the map. You can also view the attribute data of all features of a layer at once, in the form of a table. This attribute table has one row per feature and one column per attribute field, and you will use it a lot when working in GIS.







NoteSee also



How to open and use the attribute table in QGIS is explained on The attribute table.

title: 2.2 Vector model
text:
Complex, but small files
Vector files are usually small in size. After all, only the coordinates of the vertices and the attribute data have to be stored. On the other hand, the vector model is a fairly complex data structure. As a result, some spatial analyses may take a lot of computing power and time.

title: 2.3 Rasters vs. vectors
text:
A lot of spatial data can be represented as vector data as well as raster data. The choice between the two types depends on the use case.
A map with, for example, a boundary stone (point), a road (line) and a lake (polygon) would look like this as vector data (left) and as raster data (right):

VECTOR

Based on geometric objects


Spatial positioning
Each raster cell is implicitly given coordinates. This is based on the coordinates of the origin, the spatial resolution (real-world size of each cell) and the position of each cell in the matrix (row and column number).
Coordinates are explicitly stored for each point (or vertex).


File size
Usually larger files

title: 2.4 Data sources
text: Geodata (both raster and vector data) can be kept on your own computer, or on a server that you reach through a network or the internet. Below we give an overview of the data sources available in both cases.

title: 2.4 Data sources
section: Where to find and store geodata
text:
Where to find and store geodata

Local files
With local files you have your own copy of the data, which you can edit and adjust as much as you like. Because the data are on your computer, you do not need an internet connection. The downside is that this setup is not well suited for several people working on the same dataset at the same time.

Layer files
In the introduction you learned that geodata are stored in thematic layers. In its simplest form, a layer is saved as a file (or a group of files) on your computer, for example an image or a simple text file that defines vector objects. When you load such a file into QGIS, you get access to the layer it contains.


Database files
A database file can contain multiple layers and tables at once. It allows more complex data models, in which tables are linked to each other. When you load a database file into QGIS, you get access to all the layers it contains.


File formats
Technically, layer files and database files exist in several file formats, for both rasters and vectors. These formats are explained on the next page, Common file formats in QGIS. How to open them in QGIS is explained in Importing data.



Servers
Geodata are often stored on external servers: computers that share data over a network or the internet. Governments and national institutions commonly publish large datasets this way. Many people can use the same data without each downloading their own copy. You can load such data directly into your GIS.

Image and feature providers
Raster and vector data can be stored on a server and made available to users from there. From QGIS, you can connect to these providers and use their data in your map canvas, without downloading them first. The technical way in which these providers deliver their data is called a service. There are several types of services, which all deliver data but work in different ways. As a GIS user, you don’t need to know the technical details. It is enough to know that services exist and how to use them in QGIS.
Image services send ready-made map images from the data provider to your computer. Commonly used services for this are WMS (Web Map Service), WMTS (Web Map Tile Service) and XYZ tiles. Services for vector data send the vector objects themselves to your computer, together with their attributes. A widely used vector service is WFS (Web Feature Service).
Although services have clear advantages, as an end user you are limited to the permissions the provider gives you. Most providers only let you view and request data, but some also let you update them.
You will learn how to create these connections in practice in the chapter Services.


Relational databases
As explained above, a database can hold several layers and tables that can be linked to each other: this is called a relational database. A database on a server has extra advantages: many users can work in the same database at the same time, which is useful for teams and for large datasets. Such databases are also often used by web applications. How to connect to a remote database is explained in Databases.

title: 2.5 Common file formats in QGIS
text:
A format is the way in which geodata are stored in a file or database. You can usually recognise the format of a file by the file extension: the letters after the last dot in the file name (.gpkg, .shp, .tif…).
There are many formats for geodata. This page explains four of the formats you will meet most often in QGIS and in this learning path.

title: 2.5 Common file formats in QGIS
section: GeoPackage: the default for vector data
text:
GeoPackage: the default for vector data
QGIS uses the GeoPackage format (.gpkg) as its default format for vector data. A GeoPackage is a single file that can hold several layers (for example the points, lines and polygons of one project), and even rasters and plain tables. You can store not only the data themselves (for example the locations of points), but also how they are shown in GIS (for example as red stars). Because everything is in one file, a GeoPackage is easy to copy or send.
How you save several layers in one GeoPackage, convert shapefiles and save how your layers are shown is explained later, in Working with GeoPackages.

title: 2.5 Common file formats in QGIS
text:
Shapefile: older, but still everywhere
The shapefile (or Esri shapefile) dates from the 1990s, but it is still one of the most widely used vector formats: almost every GIS program can read it, and a lot of existing data are offered in it. In this learning path you will often open shapefiles, but when you save or export your own data, we use GeoPackage.
A shapefile is a combination of several files (at least three).

A shapefile always consists of:

SHP file: spatial data component
DBF file: attribute information
SHX file: an index of the geometries in the SHP file

A shapefile can also include several extra files, such as:

PRJ file: information about the coordinate reference system used
SHP.XML file: metadata
CPG file: information about character encoding







The files that form a shapefile must always be stored in the same folder with the same file name (only the extension differs, e.g. us_states.shp, us_states.dbf, us_states.shx). When you copy, move or rename a shapefile, always do it with all its files.



Compared with a GeoPackage, a shapefile has some limits:

One shapefile holds only one layer with one geometry type (only points, only lines or only polygons).
It stores only the data, not how they are shown in GIS.


GeoPackage vs shapefile

title: 2.5 Common file formats in QGIS
text:
Raster files: GeoTIFF and JPEG 2000
GeoTIFF (.tif or .tiff) is the most common format for raster data. Besides the pixel values, a GeoTIFF stores where on earth the image belongs: the coordinates of the image and its coordinate system. That is why QGIS places a GeoTIFF in the right position at once.






Not every .tif file is a georeferenced raster. A scan of an old map saved as TIFF is just an image, without coordinates. You first have to give it a position on the earth yourself; this is explained in the chapter Georeferencing.



JPEG 2000 (.jp2) files have similar properties to GeoTIFFs for storing raster data, but they are compressed, so the files are smaller. On the other hand, JPEG 2000 is generally less compatible with GIS software than GeoTIFF.

title: 2.5 Common file formats in QGIS
text:
Other formats
This page discussed the formats you will meet most often, but there are many more. Some of them, such as CSV, GeoJSON, KML and the Esri file geodatabase, are explained in the chapter Data in GIS (part 2).

title: 3.1 Importing data: vectors and rasters
text: QGIS lets you import vector and raster files, whether they are stored on your own computer or on a server.

title: 3.1 Importing data: vectors and rasters
text:
Method 1: drag and drop
The simplest way to load geodata is to drag the files onto the QGIS interface: pick up the files in a folder on your computer and drop them on the map canvas or the Layers panel. For a shapefile, which consists of several files, you only need to select the one with the extension.shp.






Drag and drop is quick, but it skips the import window with its extra settings. When you need more control over how a file is imported, use the Data Source Manager instead, as you will see later in this learning path.



If you do not want to switch between windows all the time while working in QGIS, you can use the Browser panel instead: it gives you easy access to all the folders and files on your computer.

The Browser panel has another advantage: it can also hold connections to databases and servers. In this way, you have access not only to your local files but also to all kinds of other data sources, gathered in one handy window.






GeoPackages. You can load a GeoPackage just like any other file. If it contains one layer, that layer is added immediately; if it contains several layers, QGIS first opens a window in which you select the layers you want to add.
To make working with GeoPackages easier, you do not always have to load them as a whole. Instead, you can make a connection to a GeoPackage: in the Browser panel, right-click GeoPackage ▸ New Connection… and choose the .gpkg file. When you unfold the GeoPackage in the Browser panel, you see all its layers and can add exactly the ones you need. QGIS remembers this connection, also in other projects, so you only need to create such a connection once.

title: 3.1 Importing data: vectors and rasters
section: Method 2: via the Data Source Manager
text:
Method 2: via the Data Source Manager
You can also import data into QGIS through the Data Source Manager. Thanks to its many configuration options, this manager offers a more controlled way to load geo-information. You can open the Data Source Manager by choosing Layer ▸ Data Source Manager in the menu. Alternatively, you can click the first (leftmost) button of the Data Source Manager Toolbar, if this toolbar is shown (see QGIS interface: View ▸ Toolbars).
In the Data Source Manager, the navigation column on the left lists all the data source types you can load through the manager. If you click one of these types, the configuration options for this type appear on the right. For some types, such as vector and raster files, these options are limited; for others you will have to configure more. We will give concrete examples of this in a later chapter, Data in GIS (part 2): see for example Delimited text files (CSV).
The data source types you find on the left side of the Data Source Manager are also available when you choose Layer ▸ Add Layer in the main menu. Each of these submenu items takes you directly to the right tab of the Data Source Manager.


Vector data
To load locally stored vector data, choose the Vector tab and make sure that Source Type is set to File. Then select your file(s) with the … button next to Vector Dataset(s) and click Add.






A GeoPackage is a database, but one that is stored as a file on your computer: load it with Source Type ▸ File. The option Database is meant for databases on a server.





Raster data
In the same way, you can import local raster data through the Raster tab of the Data Source Manager. Vector and raster data are thus loaded in almost the same way, but through a different tab.
Make sure you always select the right tab. Otherwise QGIS gives an error message and you cannot import the data you want.

title: 3.2 Layers in QGIS
text: Once you have loaded your data, every dataset you added appears as a separate layer. The Layers panel (C) gives you an overview of all layers in your project, and the map canvas immediately shows their spatial component. The attribute data are not shown in the map canvas straight away, but you can easily consult them (for example with Identify Features, see Navigating the map canvas, or in the attribute table, see chapter 4: The attribute table).

title: 3.2 Layers in QGIS
text:
Layers panel and map canvas







NoteSee also



Navigating the map canvas is covered on Map navigation.



The Layers panel is one of the key panels of the QGIS interface: here you find an overview of all data layers loaded in your project. 

The order in which the layers are shown in the Layers panel determines the drawing order in the map canvas: each layer is drawn on top of the layers below it in the list. This is less trivial than it may seem at first sight. 






Some layers, such as raster or polygon layers, can completely cover the layers below them and so hide them. If a layer seems to be missing from the map canvas, check the layer order first.



It is usually a good idea to keep the following order:

at the top, layers with point features
below them, the lines
below them, the polygons
raster data at the very bottom

You can easily change the order of the layers by dragging them. The checkbox in front of each layer lets you choose whether it is shown in the map canvas at all.

title: 3.2 Layers in QGIS
text:
Layer groups
If you want to bring more structure to your layers, you can add layer groups (with the Add Group button, 1 in panel C).
Layer groups not only let you organise your layers more clearly in groups that you can expand and collapse; with the checkbox of the group, you can also show or hide all its layers with one click.

title: 3.3 Navigating the map canvas
text: This page discusses three frequently used toolbars. We only cover the buttons you will use most often.

title: 3.3 Navigating the map canvas
text:
A: Map navigation toolbar (navigating)




A1
Pan Map
The leftmost button, with the hand-shaped icon, lets you use the Pan Map function. When you start QGIS, this tool is active by default. In this navigation mode you can move around the map canvas with your mouse.
You drag the map by holding down the left mouse button and moving your mouse. You can easily zoom in and out with the scroll wheel of your mouse.
This tool is widely used and will feel familiar: dragging and scrolling work just as they do in well-known online map viewers such as Google Maps, OpenStreetMap or Geopunt.


A2
Pan Map to Selection
If you click this button, the selected features (if there are any) are shown in the centre of the map canvas.
However, the map keeps the same scale (in other words, it does not zoom in or out). We will come back to the concept of scale later in this learning path.


A3
A4
Zoom In / Zoom Out
+
This tool lets you zoom in on a part of the map canvas. This makes the scale of the map canvas larger. If you click a point in the map canvas, QGIS zooms in with that point in the centre. You do not have to limit yourself to zooming in on one specific point: you can also draw a rectangle while you hold down the left mouse button. QGIS will then zoom in on this rectangle in the same way.
-
The zoom-out tool does the opposite of the zoom-in tool. With a single mouse click or by drawing a rectangle, you can zoom out in the map canvas and so make the scale smaller. The point you clicked (or the centre of the rectangle you drew) becomes the centre of the zoomed-out view. The smaller the rectangle you draw, the more QGIS zooms out.


A5
Zoom Full
The map canvas is automatically positioned so that all data fit exactly in the visible map canvas.


A6
Zoom to Selection
If you click this button, the map canvas is automatically zoomed and panned so that all selected features (if there are any) just fit in the map canvas.


A7
Zoom to Layer(s)
If you click this button, all features of the layer that is selected in the Layers panel C) are shown centred and zoomed in the map canvas.


A8
A9
Zoom Last / Zoom Next
Every time you pan or zoom, the extent of the map canvas changes: the part of the map you see. QGIS remembers your previous extents. If you accidentally move the map or zoom in or out too far, Zoom Last takes you back to the previous extent; Zoom Next takes you forward again.


A10
A11
New Spatial Bookmark / Show Spatial Bookmark Manager
With New Spatial Bookmark you save the current extent under a name. Show Spatial Bookmark Manager gives you a list of your bookmarks: double-click one to go straight to the saved extent.


A12
Refresh
Redraws all layers in the map canvas, for example when a data source has been updated outside the project but the changes have not been loaded yet.

title: 3.3 Navigating the map canvas
text:
B: Selection Toolbar (selecting features)









B1
Select Features by Area or Single Click
You can only use this tool in vector layers. With it, you can select one or more vector features.
When this tool is active, you can click one vector object in the map canvas or select several objects at once by dragging a selection rectangle. You can tell selected features apart from the others because QGIS gives them a yellow colour by default. If you have made a selection and then click a new feature, the previous selection is cancelled and a new one is made. If you want to add extra features to an existing selection, you can do so by selecting them while you hold down the Shift key. You can only select features in the layer that is selected in your Layers panel.
To remove a feature from the selection, click it while you hold down the Ctrl key.






Selections in several layers. A selection belongs to one layer. If you select features in one layer and then select another layer in the Layers panel, you can select features there too, while the first selection stays. To clear the selection in one layer, click somewhere in the map canvas where that layer has no features. To clear the selections in all layers at once, click B3.



The button also has a small arrow with other selection tools.


B2
Invert Feature Selection
Inverts the selection: everything that was selected is deselected, and the other way round. The small arrow offers other ways to select features.


B3
Deselect Features
With this button you deselect all vector features in all layers. The small arrow offers more ways to deselect.


B4
Select Features by Location
Selects features based on their position relative to other features. We discuss this in Automated selections.

title: 3.3 Navigating the map canvas
text:
C: Attributes Toolbar (querying information)




C1
Identify Features
Click a raster cell or a vector object in the map canvas to see its attribute values. They appear in the Identify Results panel; click an empty part of the map to clear it.
 
Left: a vector feature (a state). Right: a raster cell (a temperature value).
By default, QGIS only looks in the layer that is selected in the Layers panel. To include other layers, change the Mode at the bottom of the panel, for example to Top Down (all layers). If you see no results, check this setting first.


C2
Open Field Calculator
With the Field Calculator you can calculate attribute values. See Editing attribute data.


C3
Toolbox
This button opens the Processing Toolbox: a panel with hundreds of tools to analyse and edit your data. See Vector processing tools and Raster processing tools.


C4
Show Statistical Summary
Opens a tool to calculate statistics. See Statistical queries.


C5
Open Attribute Table
This opens the attribute table of the layer that is selected in the Layers panel.
Selections are linked: features you select in the map canvas are also selected in the table, and the other way round.
See The attribute table.


C6
Measure
With this tool you can measure distances, areas… Click a start point, click the next points and right-click to stop. As soon as you use the tool, a window opens in which you see the result of your measurement.

Measuring an area. Background map © OpenStreetMap contributors.



Later we will look more closely at why selections are useful and what you can do with attribute data. 






You use your mouse in the map canvas both to navigate, in different ways, and to query and select data. The tool that is active determines what clicking and dragging do. Two shortcuts work whichever tool is active: turn the scroll wheel of your mouse to zoom in or out, and hold down the space bar (or the middle mouse button) while you move the mouse to pan the map.

title: 3.4 The status bar
text:
D1
Coordinate
Shows you the coordinates of the point your mouse is hovering over at that moment. These are two values, one for the position from west to east (x) and one for the position from south to north (y). See the chapter on coordinate systems.


D2
Scale
Shows you the scale that is used in the map canvas at that moment.
The scale shows how much smaller (or, in exceptional cases, larger) the real world appears in your map canvas.
Scale is usually shown as a ratio (1:…). In the example above, the scale is 1:9280000. This means that one centimetre on your screen corresponds to 9280000 centimetres (or 92.8 km) in the real world. When you zoom in or out, you will see the scale change automatically. You can also change the scale here manually.


D3
Magnifier
Shows how much you magnify your map canvas. By default this is set to 100%. The magnifier enlarges the image in your map canvas, like a magnifying glass, but it does not zoom in: everything simply becomes larger, and you do not see more detail.






If you magnify your map canvas to, for example, 200%, the scale shown no longer matches what you see: everything on your screen is twice as large, so a scale of 1:10000 then really looks like 1:5000. Unless you have a specific reason for it, leave the Magnifier at 100%.





D4
Rotation
Shows the rotation of your map. By default, north is at the top of the map canvas; the rotation is then 0°.
If you want to change this, you can adjust the rotation. If you set 90° here, for example, west will be at the top of the map canvas. In practice, this setting is not often changed, and the convention is that north is at the top of the map.


D5
Render
While you work, QGIS keeps the map canvas up to date: every time you pan or zoom, it works out on the fly what has to be shown and draws the map again. This is called rendering. If you untick this box, QGIS stops redrawing the map canvas. This is handy when you change many settings in a large project, because you do not have to wait each time for the map to be drawn again. Tick it, and QGIS will draw the layers in the map canvas again.


D6
Current CRS
Shows which coordinate system is currently active in your project. See the chapter on coordinate systems, in particular Coordinate system of the QGIS project.


D7
Log Messages
This speech-bubble button opens the Log Messages panel, where QGIS posts messages about what it is doing: for example that a task has been completed, or a warning when a layer cannot be loaded.

title: 3.5 The QGIS project
text:
QGIS works on the principle that every work session is a project. If you save your project, you can close it and continue later exactly where you left off, without losing any work. The project file stores which data layers you use, how they are visualised, the scale and the part of the map you were looking at, the layouts you made, and so on.
 QGIS projects are saved as.qgz files, which are usually small and are meant to be opened with QGIS. Older projects sometimes have the extension.qgs; QGIS opens both.
When you start QGIS, the welcome screen lets you choose: start a new, empty project or open an existing one.

The project file stores which data layers you use, how they are visualised, the scale and the part of the map you were looking at, the layouts you made, and so on.

When you start QGIS, the welcome screen lets you choose: start a new, empty project or open an existing one.

title: 3.5 The QGIS project
text:
Project menu and toolbar
In the menu bar, the Project menu offers everything you need to work with projects: saving your project, starting a new one, opening an existing one, and more. The most frequently used actions are also available in the Project Toolbar.

Of course, there are also more advanced project settings, for example the units used for measuring distances and areas (in Project ▸ Properties…). Later in this learning path, some other project settings will come up, such as the coordinate system of the project and the Layout Manager (see General: layouts).

title: 3.5 The QGIS project
text:
Project ≠ data!
It is essential to repeat here that the data themselves are not saved in the project file: it only remembers the connections to the data sources. 






After you have saved a project, you must never delete or rename your data files, otherwise the link to the data source that is stored in the project becomes invalid. If QGIS cannot find a data source when you open a project, it shows a window in which you can point to the new location of the file (Handle Unavailable Layers).



By default, QGIS saves the location of a data source as a relative path. This means that QGIS remembers the route from the folder where the project file is saved to the storage location of the data source.
For example, if your project file is saved in the folder ‘project X’ and the data source in the subfolder vector data, QGIS will only remember that it has to look for a subfolder vector data in the folder where the qgz file is. Because relative paths are used, you can move the whole folder ‘project X’ on your computer without changing the relative position of the project file and the data sources.

Using relative paths not only gives you a little more freedom to move whole folders on your computer; it also makes it easier to send QGIS projects together with their data to other people (for example in a zip file), or to share them through a file-sharing system with local synchronisation (for example Dropbox or OneDrive).






By default, QGIS saves data sources as relative paths. If you want to change this for a specific reason, you can do so in Project ▸ Properties… ▸ General, under Save paths.

title: 4.1 The Layer Properties window
text: Every layer in QGIS has its own properties: its name, its source file, its coordinate system, and also the way it is shown on the map (its symbology). This chapter is about these properties. This first page gives a short introduction: where you find these properties, and how you can look up some basic information about a layer. The pages after that deal first with vector layers (attribute table and symbology), then with raster layers (cell values and symbology).

title: 4.1 The Layer Properties window
text:
Layer properties and actions
In The QGIS interface you saw that the Layers panel is one of the key parts of the QGIS interface: it gives you an overview of the layers you have loaded into your project. For each of these layers, you can carry out actions, look up information and configure settings.
If you right-click a layer, a menu opens with options and tools for that layer. 

The menu includes general options, such as renaming, removing, copying and duplicating the layer, or Zoom to Layer(s): the map canvas then centres and zooms so that all objects of the layer just fit in it. ( As you saw on ‘Navigating the map canvas’, this is the same function as button A7.) Vector and raster layers also have a few options of their own.
The most important configuration window for a layer, the Layer Properties, can be opened with the option at the very bottom of the menu: Properties…. 






Shortcut: double-click a layer in the Layers panel to open its Layer Properties.

title: 4.1 The Layer Properties window
text:
The Information and Source tabs
The Layer Properties window has partly different tabs for vector and raster layers. The first two tabs, Information and Source, are the same for both.

Information tab

In the first tab of the Layer Properties, Information, you will find the metadata available for the layer: for example the file size, when the file was last modified, technical metadata such as the data type, information about licences and rights (if available)…
For vector layers this tab also gives an overview of the attribute fields and their type (for example text or number). For raster layers it shows, for example, the number of columns and rows of cells (Width and Height) and the spatial resolution of the raster (A: shown as Pixel Size, the width and height of one cell, in the units of the coordinate system, for example metres).



Source tab

In the second tab, Source, you can, among other things, change the name of the layer. You can also indicate which coordinate system and (for vector layers) which text encoding (for example the widely used UTF-8) should be used.
Many of the other tabs are different for vector and raster layers. The next pages therefore discuss them separately: first for vector layers, then for raster layers.

title: 4.2.1 The attribute table
text: As you saw in The vector model, vector data combine two aspects: the geometry of each feature, which you see on the map, and the attribute data: the information linked to each feature, such as a name or a number of inhabitants. This page shows how to consult the attribute data in the attribute table, which brings together the attribute data of all features of a layer in one overview.

title: 4.2.1 The attribute table
text:
Opening the attribute table
You open the attribute table through the Layers panel: right-click the layer and choose Open attribute table. Alternatively, select the layer and press F6, or click the Open Attribute Table button on the Attributes Toolbar.

The attribute table lists all features of the vector layer (B). Each row represents one feature, and each column one attribute field. You can easily sort the rows by any attribute field, numerically or alphabetically, by clicking a column heading.
Besides sorting, you can also select features in the table: click the number at the start of a row (hold down Ctrl or Shift to select several rows). A row in the attribute table and the corresponding geometry in the map canvas are linked in the background by a shared, unique feature ID. Because the geometric (spatial) and attribute (non-spatial) properties of a feature are inseparably linked, selecting a row in the attribute table also highlights the corresponding geometry in the map canvas, and vice versa.
Editing attribute data in the table is possible too, but not by default: first switch on editing mode with the Toggle Editing button (the pencil in toolbar A). We come back to this in Editing attribute data.
A vector dataset can contain many thousands of features, and so just as many rows in the attribute table. By default you see all of them, which can make the table hard to read. That is why the attribute table has a filter function (C), which offers several ways to reduce the number of visible features, for example to only the selected ones.







NoteSee also



The filter function is explained in detail on Filtering the attribute table.



By default, you consult the attributes in a table, as shown above. QGIS also offers a form view. To switch between the two, use the buttons at D.

title: 4.2.2 Symbology of vector layers
text:
When you add a vector layer, QGIS shows it with a random colour, unless a style is stored with the data. In both cases, you can easily adapt its appearance to your needs.
You set the symbology per layer, so each layer can have its own style. You do this in the Layer Properties (see The Layer Properties window).

In the Symbology tab you decide how the layer is displayed on the map. At the top (A) you choose the type of symbology: Single Symbol displays all features in the same way, while other types give features a different style depending on their attribute values (see, for example, One style per category). At B you see which parts, or symbol layers, your symbol is made of. In this part of the window you can add and remove symbol layers and change their order. Selecting a symbol layer here opens its more detailed settings in the lower part of the window.






Often a symbol consists of a single symbol layer, but combining several symbol layers gives you a lot of freedom. Suppose you want a black square inside a white circle, for example to mark capital cities. There is no ready-made symbol for that, but there are ready-made symbols for a circle and for a square. So you can easily compile the desired marker yourself: make a first symbol layer with a white circle, then a second symbol layer with a smaller black square, and place the square on top of the circle. See the topo railway example on Configuring a style.




At C you set the basic properties of your symbol, such as its size, colour and opacity. QGIS also offers a list of predefined symbols that you can choose from.
Points, lines and polygons each have their own characteristics, so the styling options differ a little between them: points are displayed with a marker (a symbol or icon), lines with a line style and polygons with a fill. On the whole, however, the configuration works in the same way and the available options are very similar.







NoteSee also



This chapter covers the general styling techniques. Later in this learning path, once you have the necessary background knowledge, you will learn a more flexible way of styling on Rule-based styling.

title: 4.2.3 Configuring a style
text: By default, all features of a vector layer get the same style (A, Single Symbol): all points get the same marker, all lines the same line style, all polygons the same fill. You can configure in detail what this style looks like. As you saw on the previous page, a symbol consists of one or more overlapping symbol layers. For each symbol layer you choose a type (Symbol layer type). Below we discuss three widely used kinds in more detail:

title: 4.2.3 Configuring a style
text:
Simple symbols
By selecting a symbol layer in the symbol overview (B in the screenshot below), you get access to its configuration options. The first option (D) sets the type of the symbol layer (Symbol layer type), and the other options at E depend on that type.
We first explore the options for the simple symbols: Simple Marker, Simple Line and Simple Fill, for points, lines and polygons respectively. These options differ somewhat between the three geometry types, but the principle is always the same. The best way to get to know them is to try them out. The screenshots below give an overview of the configuration options for each type.
For a point layer, one of the most eye-catching configuration options is the shape of the icon used to represent a point.

For line features, besides the colour and line width, the dash pattern is often changed.

For polygons, you can change both the colour and thickness of the borders and the colour and fill pattern of the area. You can also show only the borders of your polygons and leave the area transparent. This can be useful, for example, if you want to visualise several overlapping polygons together in your map canvas.

title: 4.2.3 Configuring a style
text:
Image symbols
Sometimes a simple geometric shape is not enough: you want a church, a castle or a battlefield on your map, or a polygon filled with a texture. In that case you use an image instead. For this, QGIS offers, among others, the symbol layer types SVG Marker (for images in SVG format) and Raster Image Marker or Raster Image Fill (for images in raster formats such as PNG or JPG). You choose them in the drop-down list Symbol layer type (D).
SVG stands for ‘scalable vector graphics’. It is a widely used file format for vector images, such as icons and logos, also outside GIS.

By default, QGIS offers a large variety of typical map symbols in SVG format. You can browse them by theme in the configuration window (see F). Once you have selected the icon you want, you can also change its colour and size, just as with the simple markers. The image below shows a selection of the SVG symbols that come with QGIS.

However, you do not have to limit yourself to the symbols that QGIS offers by default. You can also load your own SVG image (at G). A huge number of SVG icons are available on the internet, but make sure you check the licence before you download and use them.
If you choose the option Raster Image Marker or Raster Image Fill under Symbol layer type, you can use images in formats such as PNG, TIF or JPG in your symbology. In this way you can choose an image file on your computer and use it as a point icon or as a fill for an area. For example, you could show a layer that represents the territory of Belgium with an image of the Belgian flag.






QGIS does not copy the image into your project; it only remembers the path to the image file. If you move, rename or delete the image, the symbol no longer works (just as with data sources, see The QGIS project). To avoid this, you can store the image in the project itself: click the small arrow next to the file path and choose Embed File….




This raster image option is available for point and polygon layers. For line layers there is a similar symbol layer type, Raster Line.

title: 4.2.3 Configuring a style
text:
Marker symbols
A marker is a point symbol. A Marker Line repeats a marker along a line, and a Point Pattern Fill fills a polygon with markers. You style the marker itself just as you style a point: it can be a Simple Marker, but also an SVG Marker or any other marker type.
In the symbol overview (B) the marker appears nested under the Marker Line or Point Pattern Fill. You therefore configure two levels:

If you select the Marker Line itself, you set where the markers appear along the line, for example at a fixed interval, on every vertex or only at the start or end of the line.
If you select the marker nested under it, you set what the markers themselves look like: their shape, size, colour and rotation.

A good example is the default line style topo railway, which shows a railway line as on a topographic map. It combines two symbol layers:

a Simple Line: the black line itself;
a Marker Line: its nested marker is a Simple Marker with a short vertical stroke as its shape, and the settings of the Marker Line place this stroke every few millimetres along the line. Together these strokes form the cross ties of the railway.

title: 4.2.4 One style per category
text:
On the previous page all features of a layer got the same symbol (Single Symbol). Sometimes, however, you want to differentiate visually between the features of one layer based on a certain characteristic: for example, show the places in the United States in a different colour depending on their class (city, town, village…).
To do this, choose Categorized in the drop-down list at the top of the Symbology tab (A). With Categorized, every value of an attribute field gets its own symbol.

Under Value (H) you choose the attribute field on which you want to base the categories. The drop-down list shows all fields of the layer: the columns of its attribute table. The attribute table of the places below, for example, contains for each place its name (NAME), its class (CLASS) and its number of inhabitants (POPULATION). In our example we categorise on CLASS.

Once you have selected the appropriate attribute field under Value (H), you can click Classify (I). QGIS then looks up all unique values of that field in the attribute table and lists them (K). Each value gets its own symbol, based on the symbol set under Symbol and with a colour from the selected Color ramp (J), by default random colours. At the bottom of the list QGIS also adds a category all other values, for features whose value does not appear in the list (for example values added to the data later).
After generating the categories, you can adjust each symbol individually: colour, shape, size… To do this, double-click the symbol you want to change under K. You can also edit the automatically created descriptive legend, which by default contains the name of the field value, by double-clicking the legend text. To delete a category from the list, select it and click the red minus button (I). To hide a category on the map without deleting it, untick the checkbox in front of it.

In some cases you do not want a separate category for every unique value, but only want to highlight a few values. Suppose, for example, that you want to highlight the places with the class city and show all other places in the same colour.

Choose the field CLASS under Value (H), as before. Do not click Classify this time, but click the green plus symbol (I). QGIS adds a new category to the list (K). Its value is still empty, so QGIS shows it as all other values.
Double-click the Value column of this category and type the value you want to highlight, in this case city.
Click the green plus symbol again to add a second category, and leave its value as it is (all other values). All features with another value, such as town or village, get the symbol of this category.
Give both categories the symbol you want.







Values must match the attribute table exactly, including upper and lower case: city is not the same as City.

title: 4.2.5 Graduated symbology
text:
Graduated numeric values are numbers that can be placed on a scale from low to high. Unlike categories such as city or village, they do not form a limited list of separate values. Attribute fields often contain such graduated numeric values, for example the population (see POP1990, POP2000 and POP2010 in the example above) or the area of a feature. In practice, this means that each feature usually has a different value: it is, for example, highly unlikely that two states have exactly the same number of inhabitants. This kind of data needs a different way of visualising than a limited set of separate categories.

To give a layer a graduated symbology, open its Layer Properties, go to Symbology and choose Graduated in the list at the top (A). For point and line layers, you then choose under Method whether the classes differ in colour (default) or in size (points) / thickness (lines); polygon layers do not have this option. The rest of the setup works similarly to a Categorized symbology: you choose the attribute field (H) and set a few style options, such as the Color ramp (J).
A Graduated symbology divides the values into classes defined by a lower and an upper limit. All features in the same class get the same symbol. QGIS offers several methods to calculate these classes automatically. You decide how this is done:

you set how many classes you want (N)
you choose how QGIS calculates the class limits under Mode (M)

Below, we discuss the options in the Mode list.

Equal Count (Quantile): each class contains (as far as possible) the same number of features. The advantage is that no class dominates the map: each symbol appears about equally often. The downside is that the classes can have very different widths: values that are close to each other can end up in different classes, while very different values can share a class. In the example, each class contains 10 states, but the last class runs from 9 to 37.3 million.

Equal Interval: QGIS divides the range of values into classes of the same width. It calculates this width by dividing the difference between the highest and the lowest value by the number of classes you asked for. The advantage is that each step from one class to the next stands for the same difference in value, which makes the map easy to interpret. The downside is that with unevenly spread values, one class can contain almost all features, while other classes stay (nearly) empty. In the example, each class is (37.3 − 0.6 million) / 5 ≈ 7.4 million wide, and 38 of the 50 states end up in the first class.

Fixed Interval: this works like Equal Interval, but the other way round: you set the width of the classes yourself under Interval size, and QGIS calculates how many classes are needed to get from the smallest to the largest value. The number under Classes is not used. In the example, an interval size of 5 million inhabitants gives 8 classes, two of which are empty.

Logarithmic Scale: the class limits follow a logarithmic scale: each class is wider than the one before. QGIS places the limits at round values on that scale. As a result, the number of classes can differ from the number you asked for. The advantage is that this method suits values that range from very small to very large, with many small values and a few large ones. In the example, QGIS makes 4 classes, with limits at 3.2 million (106.5), 10 million (107) and 31.6 million (107.5); the last class ends at 100 million.

Natural Breaks (Jenks): QGIS looks for groups (clusters) of values that lie close together: it makes the differences between the values within each class as small as possible, and the differences between the classes as large as possible. The class limits therefore usually fall in the gaps between such clusters. The advantage is that the classes follow how the values are actually distributed. The downside is that the classes have different widths, which makes the map harder to interpret. In the example, the limits lie at 3.1, 6.8, 12.9 and 25.3 million.

The result is a fixed class width with round numbers as limits between the classes. Because of this rounding, the final number of classes can differ from the number you asked for. The advantage is a legend that is easy to read. In the example, 36.8 million / 5 ≈ 7.4 million is rounded to 10 million, which gives limits at 10, 20 and 30 million and 4 classes instead of 5.

The class limits lie at fixed steps from the mean, expressed in standard deviations, for example steps of 1, 0.5 or 0.2 standard deviation. In QGIS, this method only works well when the values are spread roughly symmetrically around the mean, as in a normal distribution. With a strongly skewed distribution, such as the populations in the example, this method is in practice unusable.

text:

text:
2. Manual configuration
You can also build the classes yourself. Click the green plus symbol under the list of classes (K): QGIS adds a new class, and you set its lower and upper limit by double-clicking it in the Values column. If you started from a calculated classification, you can adjust its limits in the same way. In the Histogram tab (next to Classes) you can also see how the values are spread, and move the class limits there.






If you change the number of classes or the Mode after adjusting classes by hand, QGIS calculates all classes again, and your manual changes are lost.

title: 4.2.6 Diagrams
text: In QGIS you can show information on your map not only through the colour, size or shape of the features themselves, but also with diagrams.

title: 4.2.6 Diagrams
text:
Configuring diagrams
You set up diagrams in the Diagrams tab of the Layer Properties window. Do not forget to tick Enable diagram at the top of this tab, otherwise the diagrams are not shown on the map canvas.

At A you choose the diagram type. In QGIS 4 these are Pie Chart, Text Diagram, Histogram, Stacked Bars and Stacked Diagram (an interface to add several diagrams at once). The diagram settings are spread over several tabs (B).

In the ‘Attributes’ tab you choose which attribute fields the diagram shows. Only numeric fields can be used. To add fields, select them at C and click the green plus symbol. Each added field receives a random colour. To change it, double-click the colour at D.
In the ‘Rendering’ tab you set basic display options, such as the bar width of a histogram, the border style of the diagram…
In the ‘Size’ tab (see the image below) you set how large the diagrams are drawn. For histograms, for example, this is the length of the bars, and for a pie chart the diameter. The size is either fixed (Fixed size) or scaled (Scaled size).
With a scaled size, the size of each diagram depends on the value of an attribute field that you choose (E). Under Size or Bar length (G) you set the maximum size of the diagram (by default in millimetres). Under Maximum value (F) you can type the value that corresponds to this maximum size, or let QGIS look up the largest value of the field for you (click Find). 







If the Maximum value at F is smaller than the real maximum in the data, some diagrams are drawn larger than the maximum size at G.





In the ‘Placement’ tab you configure how each diagram is positioned on the map in relation to its feature (H). With the Over options (Over point, Over line, Over centroid), the diagram is centred on the point, the middle of the line or the centroid of the polygon. With the Around options, QGIS draws it next to that spot, at the distance you set under Distance, for example so that it does not cover a point symbol. For lines, you can also choose whether the diagram is placed above, on or below the line. Polygon layers have two more options: Inside Polygon and Using Perimeter (on the border of the polygon).

In the ‘Options’ tab you find a few settings that only apply to certain diagram types. For a Histogram, you can for example configure the direction of the bars under Bar Orientation (Up, Down, Right or Left).
In the ‘Legend’ tab you choose whether the diagram gets a legend and how it should look. The legend explains the colours, the size, or both. The labels themselves can be updated via the Attributes tab, at D (see above). The image below shows the result: a histogram per state on the map (population in 1990, 2000 and 2010), and a legend in the Layers panel that explains the colours and the bar length.

title: 4.2.7 Text labels
text:
This section covers labels that QGIS adds automatically to vector features, based on the values in their attribute fields. 







NoteSee also



Adding text to a map by hand is explained later, in the print layouts: see General: layouts.



You set up automatic text labels in the Labels tab of your Layer Properties window. Choose Single Labels in the menu to show the settings below. This default setting gives all features the same label style (font, size…). How to vary the labels between features is explained later, in Rule-based styling.

First, you decide what to label the features with: choose an attribute field under Value (A).
Then you configure the visual settings. As with diagrams, they are spread over several tabs (B).

In the tabs Text, Formatting, Buffer, Background and Shadow, you set how the text looks: font, line spacing, background… A preview at the top (C) shows the result of the current settings.
Under Callouts you choose whether QGIS draws connector lines between the features and their labels. These connectors help when you place the labels further away from the features. The QGIS documentation page gives more information.
Under Placement you set where the label is placed relative to its feature. As with diagrams, the options depend on the layer type.

Points
With Cartographic, the default for points, QGIS tries a set of positions around the point in an order that follows cartographic conventions: first top right, then top left, bottom right, bottom left, right, left… It chooses the first position that does not clash with other labels. As with Around point, you set the distance between the point and the label yourself (Distance).

The label placement options for points in QGIS, shown on Ghent.
Lines

The label placement options for lines in QGIS, shown on the bend of the Loire at Orléans. River: Natural Earth (smoothed).
Polygons

The label placement options for polygons in QGIS, shown on the state of Kentucky; blue dot = centroid.

There is often not enough room on the map for all labels without overlaps, for example when you zoom out far, or when many small features lie close together. QGIS therefore looks at the labels of all layers together, and tries to fit as many labels as possible on the map. Labels with a higher Priority (see below) are left out less easily than others. With most placement options (for example Cartographic, Around point or Free), QGIS has some freedom. In that case, QGIS solves a kind of puzzle: it tries several positions for each label so that as many labels as possible fit on the map, and takes into account the preferred position of each label (for example, top right with Cartographic). With other options, such as Offset from point, you set one fixed position for the label yourself. QGIS then has less freedom to place the labels, so that more labels can end up missing.
Further down the Placement tab, a few sections help when labels lie close together:

Label Spacing: a margin around each label in which no other label can be placed.
Duplicate Labels: with Avoid duplicate labels, QGIS does not place labels with exactly the same text close to each other, even if they belong to different features or layers. Under Settings… you set how close is too close (by default 20 mm on the map). Note that this can also hide labels you do want to see: the river and the state of Mississippi have the same name, so one of the two labels can disappear if they lie close together. Labels on the parts of one multi-part feature are a separate case, see Feature options under Rendering below.
Priority: where labels compete for the same spot, QGIS shows the one with the higher priority and can leave the others out.
Obstacles: with Features act as obstacles (on by default), QGIS tries to avoid placing labels or diagrams on top of the features of this layer. This is a preference, not a strict rule. For polygons, QGIS by default only avoids the boundary, so that labels lie completely inside or completely outside a polygon. Under Settings… you can choose to avoid the interior of the polygons instead.

Finally, under Rendering you set a few general but important display options.
Under Label options you can limit the scales at which labels are visible (Scale dependent visibility). For example, you can show the names of the major cities only when you have zoomed in far enough, so that they do not crowd the map when you look at the whole country.
Under Overlapping labels you choose a Mode: Never Overlap (the default: a label that would overlap another one is left out), Allow Overlaps if Required (QGIS first tries a less ideal position, and only lets the label overlap if there is none) or Allow Overlaps without Penalty (QGIS always uses the best position, even if labels overlap).






If some labels do not appear on the map, a common reason is that they would overlap other labels: by default (Never Overlap) QGIS leaves those out. Zoom in, or change the Overlapping labels setting. To see which labels QGIS left out, click Show Unplaced Labels in the Label Toolbar.



Under Feature options you set, among other things, whether labels are only shown when they fit completely inside the feature (polygon layers only), whether there is a maximum number of labels you want to display, and how multi-part features are labelled (Multipart geometry labeling). A multi-part feature is a single feature that consists of several separate parts, such as a state with islands.

title: 4.2.8 Style versus scale
text:
When you set the width of a line or the size of a symbol, diagram or label, you also choose a unit next to the value. The most commonly used units are Millimeters, Points, Inches and Pixels. With these units, QGIS draws the elements in exactly the size you have set, whatever the scale of the map canvas: a line 1 mm wide stays 1 mm wide, whether you zoom in or out.
With these units, lines and symbols therefore look relatively thicker and larger at a smaller scale (when you zoom out). In the overview below, the railroads cover large parts of the eastern United States, while in the detail at the bottom left (a railway junction in Arizona) they are thin, separate lines. Yet they are 0.8 mm wide in both maps.

Some units, however, work the other way round. With Map Units or Meters at Scale, you set the size in real-world units, so the symbol grows and shrinks when you zoom in and out. In the example below, the state names are 20 km high (Map Units). On the zoomed-out map (left), the name Connecticut fills most of the state, but because of the small scale, it is only a small label on the map. On the zoomed-in map (right), the name still covers the same 20 km, but now it fills almost the whole map.
