title: 4.2.8 Style versus scale
text:
Dependent on the Magnifier
The Magnifier in the status bar (see 3.4 The status bar) is different from zooming. Like a magnifying glass, it enlarges the whole map canvas and its symbology without changing the scale. At 200%, a line 0.8 mm wide is shown 1.6 mm wide on your screen, and the map itself is enlarged by the same factor.






The magnifier is useful when you want to look closely at a detail of your map as it will look at the current scale, for example on a printed map. If you zoom in instead, the scale changes and the lines can become relatively thinner. With the magnifier, the proportions between the map and its symbols stay the same.

title: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values
text: Each cell in a band of a raster layer has one numeric value or NoData (see 2.1 The raster model). A raster usually contains thousands or even millions of cells, and a cell rarely stands for a clearly delimited object, such as a building or a parcel. A list of all cells, like the attribute table of a vector layer, would therefore contain an unmanageable number of rows and tell you little. What is useful is an overview of how often each value occurs. You can get such an overview in QGIS in several ways. Below we discuss two of them: a histogram and a report of unique values.
crumbs: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values

title: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values
text:
Histogram of cell values
Open the Layer Properties window of your raster layer and go to the Histogram tab. If the histogram is still empty, you can compute it by clicking Compute Histogram. The x-axis shows the cell values (Pixel Value), and the y-axis how often each value occurs (Frequency).







If you drag the mouse over an area of the histogram, QGIS zooms in on that area. To return to the full view, press Esc.
crumbs: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values

title: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values
text:
Report of unique cell values
A second way to get an overview is a report that lists every unique value of a band, with the number of cells that have it. You create this report with an analysis tool. QGIS gathers all its processing and analysis tools in the Processing Toolbox, which by default is on the right side of the QGIS window. If it is not visible, open it from the main menu with Processing ▸ Toolbox.
Under Raster analysis, double-click the tool Raster layer unique values report. In the window that opens, choose the layer (Input layer) and the band (Band number), and click Run. When the report is ready, QGIS opens the Results Viewer panel with the report in it: click the report to open it. Besides the unique values, the report also gives the number of NoData cells.
crumbs: 4.3.1 Cell values: histogram and unique values

title: 4.3.2 Visualising raster data
text:
You set how your raster is shown in the map canvas on the Symbology (A) tab.

Under Band Rendering (B) you decide how the values in your raster cells are translated into colours. For this you choose a render type: the most common ones are explained below.
Under ‘Layer Rendering’ (C) you change the overall brightness, saturation or contrast of the colours in your raster layer.
Click ‘OK’ or ‘Apply’ (D) to apply your changes.





In 2.1 The raster model you learned that raster cells contain numeric values. What these values represent depends on the raster data. They may represent real-world quantities, such as elevation, or codes representing categories, such as soil types. In a scanned map or photograph, however, the values may represent colours rather than the real-world information shown in the image.
In the map canvas, you do not normally see the numeric values stored in the raster. Instead, each cell is displayed in a colour. To do this, the actual numeric values are translated into colours according to a set of display rules.
You can control how QGIS does this on the Symbology tab of Layer Properties. Under Band Rendering, you first choose a render type (display style). The appropriate choice depends mainly on the number of image bands in the raster and on the kind of data it contains. Below, we explain three common render types, followed by a short overview of the others.


In a colour photo or colour scan, the stored values represent colour information from the photo or scan itself. This information is stored in three image bands: one for red (R), one for green (G) and one for blue (B). Some images also have a fourth band, called the alpha band, which stores transparency information.
RGB values usually range from 0 to 255. For example, RGB (0, 255, 0) represents bright green, RGB (0, 0, 0) represents black, and RGB (255, 255, 255) represents white.
The Multiband color renderer combines the red, green and blue bands to display the image in colour. It also allows you to adjust the contrast of each band separately (B). The screenshot under General above shows these settings for a colour image of the world.



If your raster layer consists of one image band, the render types Singleband gray and Singleband pseudocolor are often used. The examples below use a digital elevation model (DEM) of northern France and Belgium: each cell contains the height of the ground in metres.
The render type Singleband gray displays cell values using shades of grey. Under Color gradient, you choose either White to Black (higher values are darker) or Black to White (higher values are lighter) (1).
Under Contrast enhancement and Min / Max Value Settings (2), you set the range of cell values used for the colour gradient. By default, QGIS uses Stretch to MinMax and Min / max. It determines the lowest and highest cell values in the raster and assigns them the two end colours of the gradient (black and white). It estimates these values from a sample of cells. Under Accuracy, you can choose Actual (slower) to use the actual minimum and maximum values.
Alternatively, you can choose Cumulative count cut (2–98%). This ignores the lowest 2% and highest 2% of values when determining the range, which often increases the contrast. In practice, you often do not need to change these defaults.

The map below shows the result with the settings in the screenshot (Black to White, minimum 0 m and maximum 806 m): the lowest areas are black, the highest white.

Elevation data: SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain).



The Singleband pseudocolor render type lets you display a single-band raster using colours other than shades of grey. You choose a Color ramp (1) and set the minimum and maximum values in the same way as for Singleband gray (2). However, this render type offers more flexibility in how colours are assigned to cell values.
You can divide the range of values into classes, either by setting the class boundaries manually or by using a classification mode and specifying the number of classes (4).
The available modes include:

Continuous (the default): QGIS creates a reference value for each colour stop in the selected color ramp. The number of colour stops depends on the ramp. For example, the single-hue green, blue and red ramps have nine predefined colour stops, while ramps such as Magma have more than 50.
Equal Interval: You specify the number of classes, and QGIS divides the range between the minimum and maximum values into intervals of equal size.
Quantile: QGIS divides the cells into classes so that each class contains approximately the same number of cells.

The table (3) lists the reference values (Value) and their colours (Color). Click Classify to let QGIS calculate the values with the chosen mode, colour ramp and number of classes, or set the values and their colours yourself: double-click a value or colour to change it, and add or remove rows with the plus and minus buttons below the table.
In addition to defining the classes, this renderer lets you choose how cell values within each class are coloured. You do this using the interpolation method (5):

Discrete: Each class is displayed using a single colour, determined by the upper boundary of the class. This works in the same way as Graduated symbology for vector layers.
Linear: QGIS creates a colour ramp between the colours assigned to the lower and upper boundaries of each class. Colours change gradually along this ramp, so cells with values between the boundaries receive intermediate colours.
Exact: Only cells whose values match those listed in the table are coloured. Cells with other values receive no colour and are displayed as transparent.


In the example above, the reference values (0, 30, 100, 200, 500 and 815 m) are set manually to emphasise differences in elevation. The lower areas are shown in several shades of green, while the higher terrain stands out in shades ranging from orange to red.

Elevation data: SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain).



QGIS 4 has a few more render types, among others:

Paletted/Unique values gives each unique cell value its own colour. It suits discrete data, such as the codes of land use or soil types.
Single color shows all cells that contain data in one colour, for example to show only where a raster has data.
Hillshade adds shading, so that the values look like three-dimensional relief. It is mostly used for elevation models.
Contours displays contour lines. It is also mostly used for elevation models.

The most suitable render type and its settings depend on the technical nature of your raster, but also on the type of data it stores. 






Use a colour gradient for a raster layer with continuous data (temperature, elevation…). If your raster contains discrete data, give each data class a clearly different colour, for example with the render type Paletted/Unique values, or with Singleband pseudocolor and Discrete or Exact interpolation. (Continuous and discrete data are explained in Raster model.)

title: 4.3.2 Visualising raster data
text:
You set how your raster is shown in the map canvas on the Symbology (A) tab.

Under Band Rendering (B) you decide how the values in your raster cells are translated into colours. For this you choose a render type: the most common ones are explained below.
Under ‘Layer Rendering’ (C) you change the overall brightness, saturation or contrast of the colours in your raster layer.
Click ‘OK’ or ‘Apply’ (D) to apply your changes.





In 2.1 The raster model you learned that raster cells contain numeric values. What these values represent depends on the raster data. They may represent real-world quantities, such as elevation, or codes representing categories, such as soil types. In a scanned map or photograph, however, the values may represent colours rather than the real-world information shown in the image.
In the map canvas, you do not normally see the numeric values stored in the raster. Instead, each cell is displayed in a colour. To do this, the actual numeric values are translated into colours according to a set of display rules.
You can control how QGIS does this on the Symbology tab of Layer Properties. Under Band Rendering, you first choose a render type (display style). The appropriate choice depends mainly on the number of image bands in the raster and on the kind of data it contains. Below, we explain three common render types, followed by a short overview of the others.


In a colour photo or colour scan, the stored values represent colour information from the photo or scan itself. This information is stored in three image bands: one for red (R), one for green (G) and one for blue (B). Some images also have a fourth band, called the alpha band, which stores transparency information.
RGB values usually range from 0 to 255. For example, RGB (0, 255, 0) represents bright green, RGB (0, 0, 0) represents black, and RGB (255, 255, 255) represents white.
The Multiband color renderer combines the red, green and blue bands to display the image in colour. It also allows you to adjust the contrast of each band separately (B). The screenshot under General above shows these settings for a colour image of the world.



If your raster layer consists of one image band, the render types Singleband gray and Singleband pseudocolor are often used. The examples below use a digital elevation model (DEM) of northern France and Belgium: each cell contains the height of the ground in metres.
The render type Singleband gray displays cell values using shades of grey. Under Color gradient, you choose either White to Black (higher values are darker) or Black to White (higher values are lighter) (1).
Under Contrast enhancement and Min / Max Value Settings (2), you set the range of cell values used for the colour gradient. By default, QGIS uses Stretch to MinMax and Min / max. It determines the lowest and highest cell values in the raster and assigns them the two end colours of the gradient (black and white). It estimates these values from a sample of cells. Under Accuracy, you can choose Actual (slower) to use the actual minimum and maximum values.
Alternatively, you can choose Cumulative count cut (2–98%). This ignores the lowest 2% and highest 2% of values when determining the range, which often increases the contrast. In practice, you often do not need to change these defaults.

The map below shows the result with the settings in the screenshot (Black to White, minimum 0 m and maximum 806 m): the lowest areas are black, the highest white.

Elevation data: SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain).



The Singleband pseudocolor render type lets you display a single-band raster using colours other than shades of grey. You choose a Color ramp (1) and set the minimum and maximum values in the same way as for Singleband gray (2). However, this render type offers more flexibility in how colours are assigned to cell values.
You can divide the range of values into classes, either by setting the class boundaries manually or by using a classification mode and specifying the number of classes (4).
The available modes include:

Continuous (the default): QGIS creates a reference value for each colour stop in the selected color ramp. The number of colour stops depends on the ramp. For example, the single-hue green, blue and red ramps have nine predefined colour stops, while ramps such as Magma have more than 50.
Equal Interval: You specify the number of classes, and QGIS divides the range between the minimum and maximum values into intervals of equal size.
Quantile: QGIS divides the cells into classes so that each class contains approximately the same number of cells.

The table (3) lists the reference values (Value) and their colours (Color). Click Classify to let QGIS calculate the values with the chosen mode, colour ramp and number of classes, or set the values and their colours yourself: double-click a value or colour to change it, and add or remove rows with the plus and minus buttons below the table.
In addition to defining the classes, this renderer lets you choose how cell values within each class are coloured. You do this using the interpolation method (5):

Discrete: Each class is displayed using a single colour, determined by the upper boundary of the class. This works in the same way as Graduated symbology for vector layers.
Linear: QGIS creates a colour ramp between the colours assigned to the lower and upper boundaries of each class. Colours change gradually along this ramp, so cells with values between the boundaries receive intermediate colours.
Exact: Only cells whose values match those listed in the table are coloured. Cells with other values receive no colour and are displayed as transparent.


In the example above, the reference values (0, 30, 100, 200, 500 and 815 m) are set manually to emphasise differences in elevation. The lower areas are shown in several shades of green, while the higher terrain stands out in shades ranging from orange to red.

Elevation data: SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain).



QGIS 4 has a few more render types, among others:

Paletted/Unique values gives each unique cell value its own colour. It suits discrete data, such as the codes of land use or soil types.
Single color shows all cells that contain data in one colour, for example to show only where a raster has data.
Hillshade adds shading, so that the values look like three-dimensional relief. It is mostly used for elevation models.
Contours displays contour lines. It is also mostly used for elevation models.

The most suitable render type and its settings depend on the technical nature of your raster, but also on the type of data it stores. 






Use a colour gradient for a raster layer with continuous data (temperature, elevation…). If your raster contains discrete data, give each data class a clearly different colour, for example with the render type Paletted/Unique values, or with Singleband pseudocolor and Discrete or Exact interpolation. (Continuous and discrete data are explained in Raster model.)

title: 5.1.1 Geographic coordinate systems
text: With coordinate reference systems (CRS) you can specify the location of every place on Earth. The two main types are geographic coordinate reference systems (global coordinate systems, discussed on this page) and projected coordinate reference systems (Cartesian or rectangular coordinate systems, discussed on the next page).

title: 5.1.1 Geographic coordinate systems
text:
Longitude and latitude
Geographic coordinate systems start from a three-dimensional representation of the Earth. Positions are defined by a latitude and a longitude, which are expressed as angles (usually in degrees).

Longitude is the angle between the prime meridian of the coordinate system (often the Greenwich meridian) and the meridian on which the measured point lies. Meridians are imaginary lines on the Earth’s surface that run through the two poles and are perpendicular to the equator. Longitude is often expressed as an angle between 0° and 180° east or west of the reference meridian.
Latitude is the angle between the plane of the equator and the line that goes from the measured point, perpendicular to the surface of the reference ellipsoid (see below), to the plane of the equator. Latitude is often expressed as an angle between 0° and 90° north or south of the equator.


A point at 50° north and 40° east.

title: 5.1.1 Geographic coordinate systems
text:
Reference ellipsoids
A geographic coordinate system describes the Earth as a three-dimensional shape. That raises a complication: there is no simple three-dimensional (mathematical) shape that represents the Earth perfectly, because the Earth’s surface is too irregular (think of the relief).
Still, many attempts have been made to define a mathematical shape that comes as close as possible to the Earth’s surface. Usually this shape is an ellipsoid, which can be described loosely as ‘a flattened sphere’. That matches the Earth: its circumference at the equator is slightly larger than along the meridians. Ellipsoids designed to represent (part of) the Earth’s surface in a simplified way are called reference ellipsoids. Over time, several reference ellipsoids have been calculated. They differ from each other in size and degree of flattening.
Some reference ellipsoids try to fit the whole Earth, sometimes at the cost of large local differences. Others were designed to fit the surface of a smaller region (such as a continent or a country) as closely as possible. For other parts of the Earth, they often deviate strongly and are therefore unsuitable there.

A strongly exaggerated cross-section of the Earth. The global ellipsoid of WGS 84 fits the Earth as a whole as well as possible. The ellipsoid used for BD72 (the International 1924 ellipsoid, positioned for Belgium) follows the Earth’s surface closely in Belgium, but deviates more elsewhere.

title: 5.1.1 Geographic coordinate systems
text:
Geodetic datum
Defining an ellipsoid’s shape and size is not enough to describe locations on Earth unambiguously. You also need to specify how the ellipsoid is positioned and oriented relative to the Earth, and the scale of the geodetic reference system. Together, the reference ellipsoid and these parameters define a geodetic datum.
A datum is a key part of a geographic coordinate system, but the two are not the same. Geographic coordinate systems can also differ in their prime meridian (which is not necessarily the Greenwich meridian) and their unit of measurement (which is not necessarily degrees).
One of the best-known examples of a global best-fit datum is WGS 84 (World Geodetic System 1984), which is used by GPS.






The name WGS 84 can refer to the geodetic datum, but it is also used for a geographic coordinate system based on it (in QGIS: WGS 84, EPSG:4326).

title: 5.1.2 Projected coordinate systems
text:
As you saw in the part about geographic coordinate systems, the Earth, or part of it, can be represented as a simplified three-dimensional object. You can also show the Earth as a map on a ‘flat’ surface, such as paper or a screen.
These flat or two-dimensional representations of the Earth are easier to produce and store. They can also show all sides of a spherical object in one image, whereas a three-dimensional representation always has a hidden side. In addition, geometric calculations (such as distances and areas) are much easier in two dimensions than in three.

To represent the surface of the Earth (and other spherical objects) in two dimensions, you use projections. The basic idea behind a projection is easy to understand if you think of light and shadows. When light shines on an object, the object casts a shadow on a surface behind it. The shadow is a projection of the object onto that surface.
A map projection uses a similar idea to represent the Earth’s curved surface on a flat plane. Imagine a light inside a transparent globe projecting the outlines of the continents onto a sheet of paper wrapped around it. In practice, map projections obviously do not use light. Instead, they use mathematical methods to transfer locations from the Earth’s curved surface to a flat map. More precisely, they convert geographic coordinates on a reference ellipsoid into coordinates on a two-dimensional plane. This process inevitably introduces some distortion. That is why a wide range of projection methods has been developed. All of them distort, to a greater or lesser degree, at least some of the true shapes, directions, distance ratios and area ratios of the map elements they show.

title: 5.1.2 Projected coordinate systems
text:
Differences between projections

Projection surface
A projection can be made onto different projection surfaces. Below, we briefly show which ones.
In a cylindrical projection, the Earth is projected onto a cylinder placed around it. Afterwards, the cylinder is ‘unrolled’ into a flat surface.

When the projection is made onto a cone, it is called a conic projection. Here too, the cone is ‘unrolled’ into a flat surface afterwards. This method is often used for areas between the tropics and the polar circles.

When the projection is made directly onto a flat plane, it is called an azimuthal projection.



Standard line
The projection surface can either just touch the Earth’s surface or cut through it. The line or point where the projection surface touches (or cuts) the Earth is called the ‘standard line’ or the ‘standard point’. A cylinder or a cone touches the Earth along one line, and a flat plane touches it at one point. When they cut the Earth, a cylinder or a cone does so along two lines, and a flat plane along one line. Along a standard line or at a standard point, there is no local projection distortion. Distortion generally increases as you move away from these locations.



Orientation
The orientation of the projection surface relative to the Earth can also vary: neither the projection surface nor the base of the cylinder or cone has to be parallel to the equator.



Position of the projection centre
Finally, the position of the projection centre can also differ.







Do not worry if a projection does not fit any of the types described above. In practice, many map projections do not correspond directly to one of these geometric types. They are defined mathematically and may be based on a geometric projection that has been adjusted, for example to reduce certain distortions.

title: 5.1.2 Projected coordinate systems
text:
Projection distortions
As mentioned above, it is impossible to show a sphere in two dimensions without distortion, so no map projection is perfect. The distortions can affect shape, direction, area and distance, and the amount of distortion varies with the position on the map. Different projection methods cause different distortions, so the best method depends on the context. Projections are often grouped according to the distortions they do (or do not) cause.

Conformal projections (angles)
Conformal projections preserve shapes locally: in other words, angles are not distorted.
The Mercator projection is probably one of the best-known examples. Gerard Mercator developed it specifically for navigation. Because the Mercator projection preserves angles locally and shows the meridians as parallel straight lines, a straight line on the map represents a route with a constant compass bearing. Navigators could follow this line to reach their destination, but usually not by the shortest route.

Conformal projections do not preserve area, and they generally do not preserve distances. In the Mercator projection above, where the standard parallel is the equator, these distortions increase towards the poles.






To see how strongly the Mercator projection enlarges areas towards the poles, try https://thetruesize.com: drag a country towards the equator or the poles and watch its size change.





Equal-area projections (area)
Equal-area projections preserve area ratios. This type of projection can be useful for showing the continents and their relative sizes.
An example is the Gall-Peters projection, which is used by organisations such as UNESCO and Oxfam.

Equal-area projections generally distort shapes and distances.


Equidistant projections (distance)
Equidistant projections preserve distance ratios, at least in one direction or relative to one or two points. No map can preserve the distance ratios between all points.
A widely used equidistant projection is the ‘plate carrée’ or ‘equidistant cylindrical projection’. It preserves distance ratios in the north-south direction (along the meridians) and along the equator, but not in other directions.

Equidistant projections are usually neither equal-area nor conformal.


Compromise projections
Some projection methods have none of the three properties above: they distort angles, distance ratios and area ratios. These are sometimes called compromise projections. They usually aim for the best possible aesthetic result and/or the smallest possible distortions of all three, without being fully correct for any one of them.
A well-known example is the Robinson projection, which National Geographic, among others, used for its world maps for many years.



Azimuthal
Because azimuthal projections use a flat plane as projection surface, they have some useful properties. They preserve the true directions from the central point of the map to every other point, and a straight line from this central point shows the shortest route. In gnomonic azimuthal projections, this last property applies to all points on the map: a straight line between any two points shows the shortest route between them on the real Earth, which is useful for navigation.

Azimuthal projections can also be conformal, equal-area or equidistant, but only one of these at a time.






For more on these distortions, watch the video Why all world maps are wrong by Vox.

title: 5.1.2 Projected coordinate systems
text:
Projected coordinate reference systems
To place map elements unambiguously on a flat map, you use projected coordinate reference systems. These systems differ from each other in several respects.

A map projection uses a mathematical/geometric formula to convert geographic coordinates on a reference ellipsoid to a flat surface.

So every projected coordinate system is based on a chosen geodetic datum (and not on the real world, which, as explained on the previous page, cannot be represented exactly by a simple mathematical shape).
This formula, in short the projection method, can also vary, as we have seen.

The result is a two-dimensional representation of the Earth in which a coordinate system positions the map elements with an x and a y coordinate.

The position of the origin (0, 0) can differ from one CRS to another.
The unit of measurement varies between coordinate systems. A widely used unit is the metre: the coordinates then tell you how many metres east/west and north/south of the origin an element lies.



Globe: NASA Blue Marble: Next Generation (public domain). Right: Belgian Lambert 72 on Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 by EOX IT Services GmbH (contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2016), CC BY 4.0. Border of Belgium: Atlas van België (NGI, ADSEI, ULiège).
Many different projected coordinate systems have been developed to limit distortions as much as possible, often specifically for a particular region.
In practice, this means choosing:

a geodetic datum that fits the real Earth’s surface closely in that area
a projection method that gives the smallest distortions for that specific area
an origin that gives convenient coordinates in that area (for example, only positive values)

title: 5.1.2 Projected coordinate systems
text:
Lambert
For maps of Belgium, two projected coordinate systems are mainly used: Lambert 72 and Lambert 2008. Both are designed specifically for this country and are therefore not suitable for areas far away from it. Much of the data you will come across for Belgium is in the older system, ‘Lambert 72’ (EPSG:31370; in QGIS: BD72 / Belgian Lambert 72): for a long time, it was the standard. However, more and more geographic datasets in Belgium are now managed and published in the newer system, ‘Lambert 2008’ (EPSG:3812; in QGIS: ETRS89 / Belgian Lambert 2008).
Both systems:

are based on a conic projection (with a cone that cuts the reference ellipsoid along two standard lines)
have an origin outside Belgium, to the south-west (a different one for each system): for Lambert 72 in the north of France (Oise), for Lambert 2008 much further away, in the Atlantic Ocean off the west coast of France
have coordinates expressed in metres.








NoteSee also



Coordinate system of the QGIS project explains how to set the coordinate system of your project, for example Lambert 72 or Lambert 2008.













Left: the cone of Lambert 72 cuts the Earth along the two standard parallels, 49°50’ and 51°10’. Right: Belgium in Lambert 72, to scale. Border of Belgium based on Atlas van België (NGI, ADSEI, ULiège).

title: 5.2.1 Coordinate system of the QGIS project
text: QGIS offers thousands of coordinate reference systems (CRSs) to choose from. As you have learned on the pages on geographic and projected coordinate systems, the choice of CRS matters: different systems represent the Earth’s surface in different ways. In QGIS, this is not just a theoretical issue. Your choice affects how your map looks and how spatial information is represented.

title: 5.2.1 Coordinate system of the QGIS project
text:
Changing the coordinate system
To change the coordinate system of your project, choose Project ▸ Properties…. You can also click the CRS code at the right end of the status bar (EPSG:31370, for example).
In the Project Properties window, open the CRS tab (A).
Select the coordinate system you want in the list (C). If it is not visible, type its name or ID in the Filter box (B).







Most coordinate systems have a unique code, the EPSG code. Choosing a system by its code is safer than choosing it by its name: some systems have almost the same name but are not interchangeable, for example BD72 / Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370) and BD72 / Belge Lambert 72 (EPSG:31300, an older variant with slightly different parameters).



Some widely used projected systems include:

For Belgium: BD72 / Belgian Lambert 72 (EPSG:31370) and the newer ETRS89 / Belgian Lambert 2008 (EPSG:3812)
For the Netherlands: Amersfoort / RD New (EPSG:28992)
For France: RGF93 v1 / Lambert-93 (EPSG:2154)
For the United Kingdom: OSGB36 / British National Grid (EPSG:27700)
For Europe: ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035), an equal-area system
For the world: WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator (EPSG:3857), as in Google Maps and OpenStreetMap. It is almost conformal and strongly enlarges areas towards the poles, so do not use it to compare or measure areas.
For a region anywhere in the world: a UTM zone. In the UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) system, the world is divided into 60 zones of 6° of longitude, each with its own projection that has little distortion within the zone. Every zone has two coordinate systems: one for the northern hemisphere (N) and one for the southern hemisphere (S). For Belgium, the most suitable is zone 31N (in QGIS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 31N, EPSG:32631).

The most widely used geographic systems are WGS 84 (EPSG:4326) for the world, as used by GPS, and ETRS89 (EPSG:4258) for Europe.
On epsg.io you can look up a coordinate system by its code, its name or a country. For each system, the website shows the area it is meant for, its unit and its parameters.

title: 5.2.1 Coordinate system of the QGIS project
section: Projected versus geographic CRS in QGIS
text:
Projected versus geographic CRS in QGIS

Projected
The projected coordinate system you choose largely determines what your map looks like, as explained on the page on projections.

Select a coordinate system that is suitable for the region you want to map. Otherwise, the distortions on your map can be large.
Select a coordinate system whose distortion properties suit the purpose of the map. If area comparisons are important, an equal-area system is a good choice. For a general-purpose map, a conformal or compromise projection may be more suitable.



Geographic
In theory, setting a geographic coordinate system for your QGIS project poses a challenge. Geographic coordinates describe positions on a curved reference ellipsoid, while the QGIS map canvas is a flat, two-dimensional plane.
That is why QGIS also applies a projection to geographic coordinate systems for display. By default, this is a cylindrical equidistant projection (plate carrée). This affects how the data are displayed in the map canvas, but it does not change the underlying coordinates of your data.






In practice, geographic coordinate systems are usually not well suited for displaying geodata in QGIS or on a map, but they are well suited for storing spatial information. For map display, choose a projected coordinate system that suits your region and the purpose of your map.

title: 5.2.2 Coordinate system of your geodata
text:
Geodata are data with a spatial component, defined by coordinates. However, because there are many different coordinate systems, the same coordinates can point to very different places.
Suppose you have a data source in which a point is stored with the coordinates 4 and 51. If your data source uses the coordinate system ‘Lambert 72’, this means that the point lies 4 metres east and 51 metres north of the origin in the north of France, near Clermont. If the same data source uses the coordinate system ‘WGS 84’, however, this means that the point lies 4° east of the Greenwich meridian and 51° north of the plane of the equator, near Dendermonde.
In other words, coordinates only have a meaning if the coordinate reference system is known.
The CRS of a data layer can be different from the project CRS. The next page, Transformations, explains how QGIS deals with this.

title: 5.2.2 Coordinate system of your geodata
section: Finding the CRS of your data
text:
Finding the CRS of your data
Often the information about the coordinate system used is included in the data source itself. A shapefile, for example, can store this information in a separate small file: the .prj file (see Common file formats in QGIS). 
Sometimes, however, this information is missing. If so, by default, QGIS loads the layer without a CRS and marks it in the Layers panel with this icon: . QGIS then cannot position the layer correctly on top of the other data. Occasionally, a layer is loaded with the wrong CRS: the data are then shown, but in the wrong place (as in the example at the top of this page). In both cases, you have to set the correct CRS yourself in the Layer Properties. 






If you use data from an external data provider and the CRS is missing, look in the metadata of the data source: the CRS is often mentioned there.



To do so, right-click the layer in the Layers panel and choose Properties…. On the Source tab (A), you can set the CRS in the section Assigned Coordinate Reference System (CRS) (B), or change it if it is wrong.







Only change the assigned CRS if the system shown is missing or wrong. Changing the drop-down list to another CRS does not convert your data to that system. It only tells QGIS in which system it should interpret the stored coordinates.
Compare it with an online translator such as Google Translate or DeepL. Imagine you want to translate an English text into Dutch. That only works if you set the input language to English. If you mistakenly set it to Dutch, the text itself does not change (it is still English), but the translator reads it as Dutch and cannot translate it correctly. In the same way, changing the assigned CRS does not change the coordinates stored in your data, only how QGIS interprets them.
On the next page, Transformations, you learn how to convert data from one CRS to another.

title: 5.2.3 Transformations
text:
Coordinates in one coordinate reference system can be converted with a mathematical formula into coordinates in another CRS. When this involves changing the map projection, the process is commonly referred to as reprojection in QGIS. More generally, it is called a coordinate transformation. 


When you explicitly reproject a layer using the methods described below, QGIS creates a new layer with the transformed coordinates. The original layer remains unchanged.
A first common way is to export the layer to a new layer with the new CRS. Right-click the layer in the Layers panel and choose Export ▸ Save Features As…. In the dialog, keep GeoPackage as Format (the default), enter a file name and choose the new CRS under CRS.

Alternatively, you can use the reprojection tools in the Processing Toolbox (Processing ▸ Toolbox). For vector layers, use Vector general ▸ Reproject layer. For raster layers, use GDAL ▸ Raster projections ▸ Warp (reproject). You can also type the tool name in the search box at the top of the toolbox. In the tool, you choose the new CRS under Target CRS (A) and, under Reprojected (B), whether the result is stored as a temporary layer or as a file on your computer.







By default, a processing tool such as Reproject layer creates a temporary layer: QGIS does not write a file, but keeps the layer in the memory of your work session. If you close your project and open it again, the content of temporary layers is no longer available.
In the Layers panel, a temporary layer is marked with this icon: . To save it as a file after all, right-click the layer and choose Make Permanent….






Besides these explicit transformations, QGIS also uses transformations implicitly. When you load data whose coordinate system differs from the project CRS, QGIS transforms the coordinates on the fly so that the data can be positioned and displayed correctly in the map canvas. This process runs in the background: the original data are not changed, but the coordinates are recalculated for display. Thanks to this, you can load data sources into QGIS and display them together, whatever their CRS.

In the Layers panel, a temporary layer is marked with this icon: . To save it as a file after all, right-click the layer and choose Make Permanent….






Besides these explicit transformations, QGIS also uses transformations implicitly. When you load data whose coordinate system differs from the project CRS, QGIS transforms the coordinates on the fly so that the data can be positioned and displayed correctly in the map canvas. This process runs in the background: the original data are not changed, but the coordinates are recalculated for display. Thanks to this, you can load data sources into QGIS and display them together, whatever their CRS.

title: 5.2.3 Transformations
text:
Transformations can lead to deviations
Coordinate transformations are not always exact. Depending on the transformation used and the accuracy of its parameters, they can introduce small positional errors, sometimes amounting to several metres or more.
Several mathematical transformations may be available for converting coordinates between two CRSs, each with its own accuracy. In that case, QGIS asks you which one to use and shows the accuracy of each. Choose the most accurate transformation that is suitable for your area.
Within one project, always use the same transformation for the same pair of CRSs. Otherwise, identical features may no longer overlap exactly. Also avoid unnecessary transformations: every transformation can introduce small inaccuracies.

title: 5.2.3 Transformations
section: Coordinate systems are not simply interchangeable!
text:
Coordinate systems are not simply interchangeable!
Although you do not need to transform geodata explicitly to visualise them in the map canvas, it is in certain cases advisable to do so.

CRS depending on the analysis
Spatial analysis tools often use the original data (and therefore the original coordinates), so the CRS of each layer affects the result:

Geographic coordinate systems are generally unsuitable for Cartesian calculations. Some QGIS tools can produce misleading results when used with geographic coordinates: a buffer distance, for example, is then expressed in degrees rather than metres (see Vector processing tools).
Not all coordinate systems are suitable for all regions. A CRS that gives reliable results for one region can show large distortions for other regions. These distortions carry over into the distances, areas and shapes the software calculates for this layer, and so lead to wrong results.
The suitable CRS also depends on the type of analysis. If you want to calculate areas for the features in a layer, a layer that uses an equal-area CRS will give reliable results; other CRSs can distort areas, especially over large regions.
If you want to run a spatial analysis on several layers (for example, calculating the overlap between two layers), using the same suitable CRS for all layers can help avoid inconsistencies and improve processing efficiency.



Why transform data explicitly?
You learned that if a layer does not use the same CRS as the project, QGIS transforms it on the fly to display it in the map canvas. This allows layers with different CRSs to be displayed together, but coordinate transformations can introduce small positional inaccuracies. As a result, the displayed position of a feature may differ slightly from its position in the original data. In addition, many analysis tools work with the coordinates stored in the layer, not with the coordinates as they appear in the map canvas. Transforming your data explicitly to a suitable common CRS can help ensure consistency, particularly when performing spatial analyses.

title: 4.4 Saving and reusing styles
text: Making a good map takes time: symbols, classes, labels, diagrams… QGIS lets you save the style of a layer, so you can create and switch between different styles for the same layer. It is also possible to copy a style from one layer to another. At a broader level, you can save the current configuration of all layers together as a map theme.

title: 4.4 Saving and reusing styles
text:
Several styles for one layer
When you style a layer, you see the changes in the map canvas as soon as you apply them. This includes not only the symbology, but also the labels, the legend, diagrams and other settings. However, you may want to create different maps from the same data, each with its own styling. Rather than having to recreate the settings each time, QGIS lets you save several named styles for the same layer and switch between them whenever you need to.
You find the styles of a layer when you right-click it in the Layers panel and choose Styles:

Add… adds a new style and gives it a name.
The list of styles shows all styles of the layer. The active one has a dot in front of it. Click another style to switch to it.
Rename Current… and Remove Current rename or remove the active style.

In the example below, the layer states has two styles: population (the population in 2010, left) and representatives (the number of representatives in 2010, right). One click in the list switches between them.







Only one style is active at a time, and every change you make is automatically stored in the active style. When you add a new style, QGIS switches to it immediately. The new style starts as a copy of the previous one, while the original remains unchanged. From then on, your changes are stored in the new style. This lets you experiment with a different look without losing your existing styling.

title: 4.4 Saving and reusing styles
section: Copying a style to another layer
text:
Copying a style to another layer
In the same Styles menu you can copy a style and paste it on another layer:

Copy Current Style copies the active style. You can copy all of it, or only a part (for example only the Symbology or only the Labels).
On the other layer, right-click and choose Styles ▸ Paste Style.

This works best when the other layer has the same geometry type and (if applicable) contains the fields the style refers to.
A style can also be saved as a file (Save Style…). You can then load it again (Load Style…), also in another project.

title: 4.4 Saving and reusing styles
text:
Map themes
A map theme stores the style configuration of the whole Layers panel at once: for every layer, whether it is visible, and which of its styles is active. A map theme does not store the order of the layers in the Layers panel.
You manage the map themes with the eye icon  at the top of the Layers panel (Manage Map Themes):

Add Theme… saves what you see now as a new map theme.
Click a map theme in the list to switch to it: QGIS shows and hides the layers, and activates their styles, as they were when you saved the theme.
Replace Theme overwrites an existing map theme with what you see now.

In the example below there are two map themes: Population 2010 (style population, with the major cities as orange dots) and Representatives 2010 (style representatives, without the cities). Choosing one of them switches the style of states and the visibility of major_cities at the same time.







A map theme only stores which style of each layer is active, not the style itself. If you change a style after saving the theme, the map theme uses the updated style, not the style as it was when you saved the theme. A map theme also cannot bring back a layer that you removed from the project: it only works with the layers that are still in the Layers panel.

title: 4.4 Saving and reusing styles
text:
Conclusion
To create multiple maps with their own styles in the same QGIS project, first give the relevant layers additional styles (Styles ▸ Add…). Then save each map configuration as a separate map theme (Manage Map Themes ▸ Add Theme…). Afterwards, you can switch between the themes to display the different maps, each with its own combination of layer styles and visibility.






Make sure you don’t lose your previous style: first create a new style, then start configuring.

title: Exercise 1: Map the Roman Empire
text:
Dataset: Roman Empire Infrastructure
In this exercise you make two maps of the Roman Empire and a print layout with both maps. You practise loading raster and vector data, layer order, raster styling, categorized and graduated styles, labels, pie charts, map themes, coordinate systems and print layouts.

title: Exercise 1: Map the Roman Empire
section: A) Map the empire and its landscape
text:
A) Map the empire and its landscape
You can do this after chapter 4.

Load all layers of the dataset. Put them in a logical order.
Show elevation: low land in green, mountains in brown or red. Use Identify to find the elevation of a city in the Alps.
Show the provinces with an outline only, so that the elevation stays visible.
Show the roads with a categorized style: major roads thicker than minor roads.
Show the cities with a categorized style on type: cities as small dots, legionary fortresses as squares. Label the cities with their name.
Save the current styles as a map theme.

title: Exercise 1: Map the Roman Empire
section: B) Map the infrastructure per province

B) Map the infrastructure per province
You can do this after chapter 4.

Restyle the provinces. Make sure you don’t lose your previous style: first create a new style, then start configuring.
Colour the provinces with a graduated style on area_km2: the larger the province, the darker the colour. Label the provinces with their name.
Add a pie chart to every province with the number of monuments of each type (n_theatres, n_amphitheatres, n_circuses, n_baths, n_temples). The more monuments in total (n_monuments), the larger the pie chart.
Save the current styles as a map theme. Switch between the two map themes to check that both maps are kept.

title: Exercise 1: Map the Roman Empire
text:
D) Make a print layout
You can do this after chapter 6.
Make a finished map, as a PDF, with:

An overview map of the whole empire, with the style of Map 2 (provinces and pie charts). This is the largest map on the page. It shows a frame with the extent of the detail map.
A detail map that zooms in on the province of Belgica, with the style of Map 1 (elevation, roads and cities).
A title, and a legend, a scale bar and a north arrow that are linked to the overview map.

title: Solution 1: Map the Roman Empire
text: This solution follows the steps of the exercise. Other choices (colours, sizes, classification modes) are fine, as long as the maps show what the exercise asks.

title: Solution 1: Map the Roman Empire
section: A) Map the empire and its landscape
text:
A) Map the empire and its landscape

Load the data. Drag roman_empire.gpkg into QGIS and select the three layers (provinces, cities, monuments). Then drag in roads.gpkg and elevation.tif. See Importing vector and raster data.
Layer order. In the Layers panel, drag the layers into this order, from top to bottom: monuments, cities (points), roads (lines), provinces (polygons), elevation (raster). The layer at the top is drawn on top. You can untick monuments for now: you do not need it for Map 1.
Elevation. Open the Layer Properties of elevation (double-click the layer) and go to Symbology.

Set Render type to Singleband pseudocolor.
Choose a Color ramp that runs from green to red or brown, for example RdYlGn. This ramp runs from red to green, so choose Invert Color Ramp in the drop-down list of the ramp: low land then becomes green and mountains red.
Click Apply. The sea is NoData and is not drawn.
With the Identify Features tool , click a city in the Alps with elevation selected in the Layers panel, for example Augusta Praetoria (Aosta). QGIS shows the value of the cell. The cells are about 4.6 km wide, so the value is an average for the area around the city, not the exact elevation of the city itself.

Provinces as outlines. In the Symbology of provinces, click Simple Fill and set Fill style to No Brush. Choose a dark grey Stroke color. The elevation now stays visible under the provinces.
Roads. In the Symbology of roads, choose Categorized, set Value to major and click Classify. Double-click the symbol of yes and give it a larger Width (for example 0.6 mm) than the symbol of no (for example 0.2 mm). You can delete the category all other values: every road has yes or no.
Cities. In the Symbology of cities, choose Categorized on type and click Classify. Give city a small dot (Simple Marker, size 1.2 mm) and legionary fortress a square (choose the square shape in the Simple Marker settings, size 2.4 mm).

Go to Labels, choose Single Labels and set Value to name.
At the scale of the whole empire, there are too many labels to read. QGIS then leaves out labels that would overlap. Zoom in on a region to see more of them. You can also show the labels only from a certain scale (Rendering ▸ Scale dependent visibility in the Labels tab): see Style versus scale.

Save Map 1 as a map theme. Click the eye icon at the top of the Layers panel (Manage Map Themes) and choose Add Theme…. Call the theme “Map 1” and click OK. See Saving and reusing styles.




Map 1: elevation, province borders, roads (major roads thicker) and cities (squares = legionary fortresses), shown in EPSG:3035 (step C).

title: Solution 1: Map the Roman Empire
section: B) Map the infrastructure per province
text:
B) Map the infrastructure per province
You make this map in the same project: untick elevation, roads and cities.

A second style for the provinces. Right-click provinces and choose Styles ▸ Add…. Call the new style “Map 2” and click OK. The new style starts as a copy of the current one (outlines only) and is now the active style: every change you make from now on is stored in “Map 2”, and the style of Map 1 stays as it is.
Graduated provinces. In the Symbology of provinces, choose Graduated and set Value to area_km2.

Choose a Color ramp in one colour, from light to dark (for example Greens).
Choose a Mode, for example Natural Breaks (Jenks), with 5 Classes, and click Classify. See Graduated symbology.
Go to Labels, choose Single Labels and set Value to name.

Pie charts. Go to the Diagrams tab of provinces and choose Pie Chart. See Diagrams.

In Attributes, add the fields n_theatres, n_amphitheatres, n_circuses, n_baths and n_temples (double-click each field, or select it and click the plus button). Give each field a clear colour and a legend name (theatres, amphitheatres, circuses, baths, temples).
In Size, choose Scaled size and set Attribute to n_monuments, the total of the five fields. Click Find to fill in the Maximum value, and set the Size of the largest pie (for example 15 mm).
In Placement, keep Over Centroid.
Click OK.

On a map with many pie charts, QGIS leaves out labels that would overlap with the pies. That is why you may see only a few province names.
Save Map 2. Untick elevation, roads and cities (if you have not done so yet), then eye icon ▸ Add Theme…, called “Map 2”. Now choose eye icon ▸ Map 1: QGIS shows the elevation, roads and cities again, and the provinces as outlines. Eye icon ▸ Map 2 brings back the graduated provinces with the pie charts.




Map 2: provinces coloured by area, with pie charts of the monuments per type (theatres blue, amphitheatres orange, circuses red, baths purple, temples grey); the size shows the total number. Shown in EPSG:3035 (step C).

title: Solution 1: Map the Roman Empire
text:
C) Prepare for finishing

A suitable coordinate system. Choose Project ▸ Properties…, go to CRS, type 3035 in the Filter box, select ETRS89-extended / LAEA Europe and click OK. QGIS now transforms all layers on the fly. The provinces in the north (Britannia, Germania) are no longer stretched in width, as they are in EPSG:4326, and the empire looks as it does on a globe. EPSG:3035 is made for Europe: the provinces furthest away (Aegyptus, Mesopotamia) are a little more distorted, but much less than in EPSG:4326. It is also an equal-area projection, which suits Map 2, where the colours show the area of the provinces. See Coordinate system of the QGIS project. If QGIS asks which transformation to use, keep the proposed one.
Save the project. Choose Project ▸ Save As… and save the project in the folder of the dataset, for example as roman_empire.qgz. The project only stores where the data are and how they look, not the data themselves: see The QGIS project. Keep the project: the next exercise continues with it (layout).

title: Solution 1: Map the Roman Empire
text:
D) Make a print layout
Open the project of steps A–C. See also the chapter on layouts.

New layout. Choose Project ▸ New Print Layout… and give the layout a name.
Overview map. Choose Add Item ▸ Add Map and drag a large rectangle on the page. In the Item Properties of this map, under Layers, tick Follow map theme and choose “Map 2”. Zoom the map to the whole empire.
Detail map. Add a second, smaller map in the same way. Let it follow the map theme “Map 1”. In the main QGIS window, zoom in on the province of Belgica. Back in the layout, click Set Map Extent to Match Main Canvas Extent in the Item Properties of the detail map.
Extent frame. Select the overview map. Under Overviews, click the plus button, and under Map frame choose the detail map. The overview map now shows a frame around the area of the detail map.
Title, legend, scale bar and north arrow.

Add a title with Add Item ▸ Add Label.
Add a legend with Add Item ▸ Add Legend. In its Item Properties, choose the overview map as the map it is linked to. Remove the legend items you do not need, or tick Only show items inside linked map.
Add a scale bar with Add Item ▸ Add Scale Bar and link it to the overview map. If the numbers are long and overlap, set Scalebar units to Kilometers.
Add a north arrow with Add Item ▸ Add North Arrow. Under Image Rotation, tick Sync with map and choose the overview map.

Export. Choose Layout ▸ Export as PDF….
